# 01_cover

[Opening] Welcome. Today's briefing addresses one of the most underestimated public health challenges of our time — the global burden of mental illness.

We'll walk through eight slides that take you from the scale of the problem to the core data, the treatment gap, and actionable policy implications. All figures are drawn directly from the IHME Global Burden of Disease 2025 dataset, as synthesized by Our World in Data.

[Pause]

Key points: (1) Set the evidence-based, data-forward tone (2) Establish source credibility — IHME GBD 2025 (3) Signal policy relevance for this audience
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_mental_health_scale

[Transition] Let's begin with the scale. These two numbers — 1 in 3, and 1 in 5 — are the foundation for everything that follows.

One in three women will experience major depression at some point in their lifetime. [Pause] One in five men. These are not marginal probabilities — they are the lived reality of a significant portion of any population your programs serve.

[Data] 1 in 3 — that is roughly 33%. Think about any policy audience, any community. One third of the women in that room.

Beyond depression and anxiety, conditions like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder affect fewer people — but at devastating individual severity. The challenge is not just breadth, it is depth.

[Scan Room] Before we move to the disease burden data, are there questions on these prevalence figures?

Key points: (1) 1-in-3 women / 1-in-5 men lifetime depression risk (2) Spectrum from common to severe conditions (3) Frame why this demands systemic policy response
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_burden_by_category

[Transition] Now let's quantify that burden precisely. This chart is the central evidence slide for today's briefing.

We're measuring in DALYs — disability-adjusted life years per 100,000 people. This metric captures both premature death and years lived with disability, giving us a comprehensive picture of burden. [Data]

Depressive disorders: 694.6 DALYs. Anxiety disorders: 686.5 DALYs. [Pause] Look at the bars. They are virtually the same length. The difference is just 8.1 DALYs — statistically near-identical.

[Benchmark] Schizophrenia, at 210.2, is less than one-third of the depression figure. Bipolar at 94.6, eating disorders at 47.5 — meaningful, but a fraction of the two dominant conditions.

The strategic implication is clear: any mental health resource allocation that ignores depression and anxiety at scale is misaligned with the actual burden distribution.

Key points: (1) Exact DALY figures from IHME GBD 2025 (2) Depression and anxiety near-identical in burden (3) Schizophrenia and bipolar are lower population-burden but not negligible
Duration: 2.5 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, read the top three values and move on — the visual does the work]

---

# 04_depression_vs_anxiety_parity

[Transition] Let's zoom into that near-parity between depression and anxiety — because the policy implications of this equivalence are often underappreciated.

694.6 versus 686.5. [Pause] A difference of 8.1 DALYs per 100,000. For all practical purposes, these two conditions carry identical population-level burden.

[Benchmark] Together, they represent roughly 59% of the total mental health disease burden across the five main categories we're examining. They dwarf everything else combined.

The core insight here: many health systems have historically prioritized either depression or anxiety in program design. The data says both must be primary targets — simultaneously, at equivalent resource intensity.

Key points: (1) 8.1 DALY difference — functionally indistinguishable (2) Combined ~59% of 5-category burden (3) Both must be co-equal policy priorities
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_severe_conditions

[Transition] Having established where the bulk of the population burden sits, we must now address a critical equity question: what about the people with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder?

210.2 DALYs for schizophrenia. 94.6 for bipolar. [Data] These numbers are smaller than depression and anxiety — but the per-person story is very different.

[Scan Room] Schizophrenia typically manifests in late teens or early twenties. It involves psychosis, cognitive impairment, and negative symptoms that can last a lifetime. The DALYs per affected individual are among the highest of any condition.

Bipolar disorder is frequently misdiagnosed initially as depression. Delays in correct diagnosis mean delays in effective treatment — episodes accumulate, and functional impairment compounds.

The policy implication: scaling primary care for common disorders is necessary but not sufficient. Specialized psychiatric capacity, community integration, and long-term support systems must be preserved and funded.

Key points: (1) Schizophrenia 30% of depression burden but concentrated in severely impaired individuals (2) Bipolar 14% — high individual severity, diagnostic delay common (3) Specialized care is non-negotiable alongside primary care scaling
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_treatment_gap

[Transition] We've now established what the burden is. The next question is: what is the system response?

Mental illnesses are treatable. The evidence base for this is strong — pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, and psychosocial interventions all have efficacy. And yet, a large treatment gap persists.

[Pause] Four key barriers.

Stigma: People are uncomfortable disclosing symptoms — to clinicians, to family, even to themselves. This means help-seeking is suppressed, and our data on true prevalence is likely an underestimate.

Access: Treatment is often lacking, especially in LMICs where mental health spending per capita can be under one dollar per year.

Quality: Even where treatment exists, the evidence base may not be applied — underdosed medications, inadequate psychotherapy, undertrained providers.

Underreporting: The same stigma that prevents help-seeking distorts our epidemiology. [Data] If anything, the 694 and 687 DALY figures we discussed earlier are floors, not ceilings.

Key points: (1) Treatments exist and are effective (2) Four-barrier framework: stigma, access, quality, underreporting (3) True burden likely higher than measured
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_coping_and_response

[Transition] Given the treatment gap, how do people actually cope? Global survey data gives us a clear and sobering picture of the diversity of responses.

Three dominant strategies: prescribed medication, religious or spiritual activities, and talking to friends and family.

[Benchmark] In high-income countries, the medical pathway dominates. In many lower-income settings, the primary coping resource is community and faith — not because people prefer it over clinical care, but because clinical care is unavailable.

[Data] Talking to friends and family is the most universally reported mechanism — it transcends income level and healthcare system. But it is not a clinical substitute.

The core insight here is that policy must be culturally contextualized. Interventions that ignore local coping frameworks will face adoption barriers. Programs that integrate them have a stronger implementation foundation.

Key points: (1) Three strategies: medication, spiritual, social support (2) Strategy mix varies by income setting (3) Cultural context is a program design prerequisite, not an afterthought
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways_and_implications

[Transition] Let me close with five takeaways that I hope will frame your policy decisions going forward.

First: depression and anxiety represent the overwhelming majority of mental health DALYs — approximately equal in burden, and together accounting for well over half of total measured burden. Resource allocation should reflect this.

Second: schizophrenia and bipolar carry disproportionate individual severity. Scaling up common-disorder services must not come at the cost of dismantling specialist care.

Third: treatments work — but the access and quality gaps are large and persistent. This is a systems problem, not a knowledge problem.

Fourth: stigma suppresses both help-seeking and data quality. Anti-stigma interventions are upstream investments that improve everything downstream.

Fifth: culturally adapted, task-shifted interventions for depression and anxiety at primary care level — alongside sustained specialist capacity — represent the evidence-based policy direction. [Pause]

[Scan Room] I'm happy to go deeper on any of these five points, or on the underlying DALY data. Thank you.

Key points: (1) Five structured takeaways covering burden, severity, access, stigma, and policy direction (2) Pyramid conclusion: depression/anxiety at scale + specialized care for severe conditions (3) All data sourced from IHME GBD 2025 / Our World in Data
Duration: 2 minutes

The deck follows the full ppt-master pipeline end-to-end: Exhibit-style dark/light hybrid theme with teal-to-blue gradient branding, exact DALY figures from `source_brief.md`, horizontal bar chart for burden-by-category, side-by-side paired bars for the depression/anxiety parity slide, large callout numbers (1-in-3/1-in-5) on the prevalence slide, and a 2×2 icon infographic for the treatment gap — all with conclusion-first takeaway bars throughout.
